name: AWE Aldermaston
description: Site described by the regulator as covering the entire life cycle of nuclear warheads: research, design, component manufacture and assembly, in-service support, decommissioning.
source: Office for Nuclear Regulation, defence sites: AWE Aldermaston

name: AWE Burghfield
description: Site where, in the regulator's words, warheads are assembled and maintained while in service and decommissioned when out of service.
source: Office for Nuclear Regulation, defence sites: AWE Burghfield

name: Sellafield (Windscale piles and Calder Hall)
description: Windscale piles produced military plutonium until the 1957 fire; the Calder Hall reactors produced military plutonium until 1989. Now a decommissioning and waste site.

name: Chapelcross
description: Reactors used to produce plutonium until 1964 and tritium thereafter; shut down 2003–2004.

name: Capenhurst (gaseous diffusion plant)
description: Gaseous diffusion plant that produced HEU for weapons from 1952 to 1962, then LEU for power reactors until 1982. The centrifuge plant on the same site is civil (Urenco).

name: CEA/DAM Île-de-France (Bruyères-le-Châtel)
description: CEA centre that, in its own description, designs the nuclear charges of France's deterrent weapons and guarantees their safety and reliability; also hosts the DAM's high-performance computing.

name: CEA Valduc
description: CEA centre that processes and recycles the materials for the nuclear sub-assemblies of the deterrent's weapons, and operates the Epure radiographic facility under the France–UK defence treaty.

name: CEA Le Ripault
description: CEA centre that designs and manufactures materials for the non-nuclear components of the deterrent's weapons, including pyrotechnic sub-assemblies and warhead casings.

name: CEA CESTA
description: CEA centre responsible, in its own description, for the overall design of the warheads of the French deterrent; operates the Laser Mégajoule.

name: Marcoule (G1–G3, Célestin, Phénix)
description: Graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors G1–G3 produced plutonium until 1992; the two Célestin reactors (1967/1968–2009) and the Phénix fast reactor also produced weapon plutonium. Site continues as a civil research and waste-management centre.

name: Pierrelatte (military enrichment plant)
description: HEU production ended in June 1996; the plant was shut down and is being dismantled. The Georges Besse II centrifuge plant on the Tricastin site is civil.

name: China Academy of Engineering Physics (CAEP)
description: Research academy in Mianyang described by FAS as the primary design laboratory for Chinese nuclear weapons; on the U.S. Commerce Entity List since 1997 with its subordinate institutes.
source: Federation of American Scientists, China nuclear forces guide: CAEP
coord_note: coordinate as given by FAS (31°28'N 104°46'E), tier 2

name: Lop Nur nuclear test site
description: China's nuclear test site; the Bulletin's Nuclear Notebook reports construction at the site and U.S. statements of concern about adherence to a zero-yield standard.
source: Kristensen, Korda et al., Chinese nuclear weapons, 2025, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (Nuclear Notebook)
coord_note: Lop Nur lake centroid, not the test base

name: Jiuquan Atomic Energy Complex (Plant 404)
description: Plutonium production reactor believed shut down in 1984; the complex continues with reprocessing capacity.

name: Guangyuan plutonium production complex (Plant 821)
description: Reactor that, per IPFM, probably stopped plutonium production by 1989.

name: Lanzhou gaseous diffusion plant (Plant 504)
description: Produced HEU for weapons; now operates as a civil enrichment facility producing LEU.

name: RFNC-VNIIEF (Sarov)
description: Nuclear weapon laboratory listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007 among the enterprises of the nuclear weapons complex.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: RFNC-VNIITF (Snezhinsk)
description: Nuclear weapon laboratory listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: VNIIA (Dukhov Institute), Moscow
description: Institute for warhead design and non-nuclear components listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: Elektrokhimpribor (Lesnoy)
description: Weapon assembly and disassembly plant listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: Instrument-Building Plant (Trekhgorny)
description: Warhead assembly and disassembly plant listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: PO Start (Zarechny)
description: Weapon disassembly facility listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: Novaya Zemlya test site
description: Nuclear test site listed in Presidential Decree No. 556 of 27 April 2007.
source: Podvig, Russian strategic nuclear forces blog: Presidential decree lists Russia's military nuclear facilities (Decree No. 556, 27 April 2007)

name: Siberian Chemical Combine (Seversk)
description: Plutonium production reactors at Seversk, all closed (IPFM lists every Russian production reactor as closed; the Seversk reprocessing plant closed in 2010). The isotope-separation plant continues to produce LEU.

name: Mining and Chemical Combine (Zheleznogorsk)
description: Plutonium production reactor ADE-2 shut down in April 2010; a pilot demonstration reprocessing centre operates on the site.

name: Khushab production reactors
description: Four production reactors at which, per IPFM, Pakistan's plutonium has been produced.
coord_note: Khushab city centroid, not the complex

name: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (CIRUS, Dhruva)
description: CIRUS (40 MWt) produced weapon-grade plutonium and was shut down in 2010; Dhruva (100 MWt), commissioned 1985, continues to operate. A pilot-scale enrichment plant began operating in 1985.

name: Dimona reactor (Negev Nuclear Research Center)
description: Israel does not confirm or deny a weapons program. IPFM describes a plutonium production reactor that is still operating and may now be run primarily for tritium production.

name: Yongbyon 5 MWe reactor and experimental LWR
description: The 5 MWe reactor resumed operation in 2021; a light-water reactor under construction since 2010 appeared to begin operating in late 2023, per the Nuclear Notebook.
source: Kristensen, Korda et al., North Korean nuclear weapons, 2024, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (Nuclear Notebook)

name: Punggye-ri nuclear test site
description: Test site partially disabled in May 2018; the Nuclear Notebook reports reconstruction since 2022. No test has occurred since 2017.
source: Kristensen, Korda et al., North Korean nuclear weapons, 2024, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (Nuclear Notebook)

name: Hanford Site
description: Produced plutonium for weapons from 1943 to 1987; only N Reactor operated after 1971. Its mission since has been cleanup under the 1989 Tri-Party Agreement.
source: U.S. Department of Energy, Hanford Site history
